title: NEAT: Neighborhood-Guided, Efficient, Autoregressive Set Transformer for 3D Molecular Generation
claim: A generation step decomposes into a shared representation feeding a discrete type prediction and a continuous position prediction, extending the structure one element at a time.
layout: 2 columns, loops bottom-up then right, numbered colored steps, probabilities under boxes
description: The figure shows one autoregressive generation step for a 3D molecule. The left column is titled 'Molecule at state n' and the right column 'Molecule at state n+1'. Each has a ball-and-stick molecule render, and the right one has one extra atom. Under the left molecule are the inputs a_{1:n}, X_{1:n}. They go down through a 'Set Transformer' box, then a pink bar for the abstract representation z_n, labeled (1) in red. From the bar, an arrow goes down to a 'Linear & Softmax' box and then to a table of atom-type probabilities (H, C, N, O) with C highlighted yellow, labeled (2) in orange. Another arrow goes right to a 'Flow head' box. Its output is a blue coordinate vector, labeled (3) in blue. That vector leads up to the updated molecule. Conditional probability formulas sit beside each stage.
caption: Autoregressive generation of 3D molecules with NEAT. (1) A set transformer produces an abstract representation zn of the molecule at state n, given the atom types a1:n and the coordinates X1:n. (2) The next atom type an+1 is inferred from zn. (3) The next atom position xn+1 is modeled via a flow head, which concludes the molecule update at state n + 1.
abstract: Transformer-based autoregressive models offer an efficient alternative to diffusion- and flow-based approaches for generating 3D molecules. One challenge remains: standard transformer architectures require a sequential ordering of tokens, which is not inherently defined for the atoms in a molecule. Prior works have addressed this by using canonical atom orderings. However, these approaches are not permutation invariant w.r.t. atoms and bias next-token prediction towards ordering conventions. We overcome this limitation by introducing a novel neighborhood-guided training strategy. Our model, NEAT (Neighborhood-Guided, Efficient, Autoregressive Set Transformer) treats molecular graphs as sets of atoms and learns an order-agnostic distribution over admissible tokens at the graph boundary, thereby ensuring atom-level permutation invariance. NEAT achieves state-of-the-art generation quality on the QM9 and GEOM-Drugs datasets, enables seamless completion of molecular prefixes, and offers a significant speed advantage over existing baselines.
